indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.3.1.1: Recognise that different parts of the human body work independently to perform a specific function
indicator.objective: Explain that the external parts of the human body work interdependently to perform a function

skills.description: Explain that different body parts work together (interdependently) to perform a task
Give examples of how parts work together
Explain why it is important for body parts to work together
Describe how specific parts cooperate in a given scenario

misconceptions: Body parts work completely alone and do not need each other.
Only the legs are needed to play football.
The eyes are not needed for walking.
If one part is missing, the others cannot do anything at all.

questions.stem: Which body parts work together when you clap your hands?
hints: They are at the end of your arms.
questions.explanation: When you clap, both of your hands work together to make a sound.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you clap with your legs.

questions.stem: Which parts of your body work together to help you walk?
questions.explanation: Your legs and feet work together to help you walk, run, and jump.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think eyes are the most important for walking, but legs and feet do the movement.

questions.stem: When you read a book, which two body parts work together most closely?
hints: You think about what they mean.
questions.explanation: Your eyes see the words, and your brain helps you understand them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the mouth is needed for reading.

questions.stem: When you smell a flower, your nose sends messages to your...
hints: It helps you understand the smell.
questions.explanation: Your nose detects the smell, and your brain helps you recognise it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the nose does all the work alone.

questions.stem: Which body parts work together to help you eat a bowl of rice?
hints: You use a spoon with one part.
questions.explanation: Hands hold the spoon, the mouth takes in food, and teeth chew it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may forget the role of hands in eating.

questions.stem: Kofi is kicking a football. Which body parts are working together?
questions.explanation: Kofi's eyes help him see the ball, and his legs help him kick it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may only think of the legs.

questions.stem: Ama is sweeping the floor. Which parts of her body are she using together?
questions.explanation: Ama uses her hands to hold the broom and her eyes to see where to sweep.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider the eyes as part of physical chores.

questions.stem: When you are listening to a story on the radio, what parts are working together?
questions.explanation: Your ears hear the sound, and your brain helps you understand the story.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think listening only involves the ears.

questions.stem: Kwame is riding a bicycle. His hands are steering, and his legs are...
questions.explanation: Kwame's hands steer the bike while his legs pedal to make it move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the hands and legs do the same job.

questions.stem: Why is it important for your eyes and hands to work together when you catch a ball?
options: Your eyes see the ball and your hands catch it
hints: You need to see where the ball is.
questions.explanation: Eyes track the ball's movement, and hands move to catch it. They must work together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think catching is only about hands.

questions.stem: Why do your ears and eyes work together when you cross a busy road?
options: You see the cars and hear them coming
questions.explanation: You use your eyes to see oncoming traffic and your ears to hear vehicles approaching, helping you cross safely.
questions.misconception: Pupils may rely only on sight.

questions.stem: Why do your nose and mouth work together when you have a cold?
options: They both help you breathe when your nose is blocked
hints: When you are sick, you cannot breathe well through your nose.
questions.explanation: When your nose is blocked, your mouth helps you breathe, showing how they work together for survival.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only the nose is for breathing.

questions.stem: Ama says 'I only use my legs to play football.' Why is she wrong?
options: She also uses her eyes, arms, and brain to play
She actually uses only her arms
hints: How does she see the goal?
How does she keep her balance?
questions.explanation: Playing football requires many parts: legs to run and kick, eyes to see, arms for balance, and the brain to make decisions.
questions.misconception: Pupils may oversimplify physical activities to one body part.

questions.stem: When you hold a hot cup of tea, your hand feels the heat and you quickly pull it away. Which parts work together here?
hints: The brain tells the hand to move.
questions.explanation: The hand senses the heat and sends a message to the brain, which tells the hand to pull away.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize the brain's role in reflex actions.

questions.stem: Kofi is carrying a bucket of water on his head. Which parts of his body are working together to keep him balanced and moving?
hints: He uses his neck to balance the bucket.
He uses his legs to walk.
He uses his eyes to see the path.
questions.explanation: The neck supports the bucket, legs provide movement, and eyes guide the way.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider the neck's role in carrying loads.

questions.stem: How do your mouth and nose work together when you are eating a delicious meal?
options: Your nose smells the food while your mouth tastes and chews it
hints: You smell the food before eating.
You taste it when you eat.
questions.explanation: The nose detects the aroma, and the mouth tastes and breaks down the food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think taste and smell are completely separate.

questions.stem: To write a sentence on the board, which body parts work together?
hints: Your brain thinks of the words.
questions.explanation: Eyes guide the hand, the hand writes, and the brain forms the sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think writing is only about the hand.

questions.stem: If a person loses their eyesight, which other body parts might they use more to help them navigate their environment?
hints: They might touch things to feel them.
They might listen carefully for sounds.
questions.explanation: People who are blind often rely more on their hands to feel their surroundings and their ears to listen for cues.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think losing sight means all other senses stay the same without adaptation.

questions.stem: If you break your leg, how do your other body parts work together to help you move around?
options: Arms and hands help you use crutches or a wheelchair
Your ears help you balance on one leg
hints: You might hold onto something for support.
questions.explanation: When one leg is injured, the arms and hands take on extra work to support the body using crutches or a wheelchair.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think losing the use of one part stops all movement.

questions.stem: Ama broke her right arm. How does her left arm work interdependently to help her eat?
options: The left arm holds the food or spoon for her
The left arm chews the food
The left arm helps her see
The left arm helps her hear
hints: She can still use her good arm.
It takes over the work of the injured arm.
questions.explanation: Body parts can adapt and compensate for an injured part, showing how they work together to achieve a goal (eating).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think an injured arm stops all eating activities.
